hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? has something happened this year that you still can’t explain?
options: then hold it gently while we watch. this one is old, and kind.
keep them in mind. this story has a lot of small turns.
good. keep this one for the day you need it.

steps.line: Over two thousand years ago, a Chinese book called the Huainanzi told of an old man who lived near the northern frontier, with his son and their horses.
One day his horse ran off across the border. The neighbors came to comfort him. What bad luck!

steps.q: The neighbors say it’s bad luck. What do you think the old man says?
o: “Who knows? This could be good luck”
steps.why: “How do you know this won’t turn out to be a blessing?” He doesn’t argue. He just won’t decide yet.

steps.line: Months later, the horse came home, bringing fine horses from beyond the border. What good luck! the neighbors said. Who knows, said the old man, this could be bad luck.

steps.q: Things just got better. Why would the old man still say it could be bad luck?
o: One moment can’t show how it turns
He’s gloomy and expects the worst
He never wanted the new horses
steps.why: He isn’t gloomy. He’s honest. From inside one moment, you can’t see where it leads.

steps.line: His son loved riding the new horses. He fell, and broke his leg, and was left with a limp. What bad luck! Who knows, said the old man.

steps.q: A year later, an army crosses the border and the young men are called to fight. What happens to the son?
o: He goes and becomes a hero
He runs away into the hills
His injured leg keeps him home, safe
steps.why: Nine in ten of the frontier men died. The son, with his limp, stayed home, and lived.

steps.line: A year later, raiders invaded. The young men took up bows to fight, and nine in ten frontier men died. The son, with his limp, stayed home.

steps.q: The Huainanzi describes the old man as skilled at one thing. What?
steps.why: The book calls him a man skilled in reading signs. Many readers enjoy the irony: the expert in signs is the one who says, who knows?

steps.line: Today, people retell it as the farmer who only ever says “maybe.” It’s an old answer to “everything happens for a reason.”
steps.label: today

steps.q: The neighbors got it wrong every single time. What was their mistake?
o: They were jealous of the old man
They judged each turn as the last word
They didn’t know much about horses
steps.why: Each “what luck!” closed the story too early. The Huainanzi’s own lesson: good fortune turns to bad and bad to good, and you can’t see where it ends.

say: here’s what i love. the old man never says why. he says, who knows? the book, which draws deeply on daoist thought, ends with its lesson: good fortune turns into bad, and bad into good, without end.
so you don’t need the reason to make your next move. not why, but what now. that question always has an answer.

steps.q: A friend loses a job and says, “everything happens for a reason, right?” What would the old man’s way sound like?
o: “Don’t worry, it’ll turn out good. It always does”
“Who knows yet? It’s too soon to call it”
“No. Sometimes things are just bad luck”
steps.why: He never promised the bad would turn good, and he never called it final either. He left the story open.

today.say: when something goes wrong today, even something small, try the old man’s words before you judge it: who knows? then ask, what now?
options: lovely. one “who knows” at a time.
I’ll save it for something bigger
that counts. the old man waited too.

card.from: a Chinese teaching story, from the Huainanzi
sources: Huainanzi, chapter 18 (“Renjian xun”, Among Men): the old man near the frontier (sai weng) whose horse runs off to the Hu lands, returns with Hu horses, the son breaks his leg (thigh) riding, a year later the Hu invade, nine of ten men near the frontier die, father and son survive; closing line that fortune and misfortune turn into each other without end.
English: John S. Major et al., The Huainanzi (Columbia University Press, 2010), chapter 18.
Proverb 塞翁失马，焉知非福 (“the old man of the frontier lost his horse; how do you know it isn’t a blessing?”) derives from this passage.
